questions.q: According to this lesson, what practical question is the platform team trying to answer by combining DORA, SPACE, and its own platform telemetry?
options: Which developer survey platform to purchase for next year
Given everything the combined signals show, what should the platform team actually build next
How to format the quarterly board presentation slides
Which cloud provider offers the cheapest CI runner pricing
questions.explain: The whole point of collecting delivery, experience, and platform-health signals is to answer one practical prioritization question each planning cycle, rather than guessing or defaulting to the loudest request.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, lead-time data shows every pipeline stage is fast except a manual security sign-off that sits open for two days. What does this metric point to building next?
options: A brand-new developer onboarding portal
A survey to ask developers how they feel about security reviews
Automating that specific approval gate with policy-as-code checks or giving it a committed SLA
A platform-wide rewrite of the CI/CD system from scratch
questions.explain: When lead-time data isolates a specific bottleneck — here, a slow manual approval gate — the targeted fix is to automate or SLA that exact gate, not launch an unrelated platform-wide initiative.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend targeting a fix at one specific team's pipeline when that team's change failure rate is three times the org average, rather than launching a platform-wide initiative?
options: Because aggregate DORA numbers can hide a problem concentrated in one pipeline, so a platform-wide response would be the wrong scope for a localized issue
Because platform-wide initiatives are always more expensive regardless of the data
Because change failure rate cannot be measured per team, only org-wide
Because only one team is allowed to use canary deployments under the platform's policy
questions.explain: A high change failure rate concentrated in one pipeline is a localized problem that aggregate metrics can mask; the lesson calls for a targeted fix — better test coverage or progressive delivery for that specific pipeline — not a broad initiative.

questions.q: What does Goodhart's law describe, as applied to a platform team's own roadmap decisions?
options: That GitOps controllers always reconcile faster than CI runners can dispatch jobs
That developer satisfaction surveys are statistically unreliable below a certain sample size
That lead time and deployment frequency are mathematically impossible to measure at the same time
That once a measure becomes an explicit target, people optimize the measure itself — for example splitting trivial changes into extra deploys just to move a deployment-frequency number
questions.explain: Goodhart's law is the principle that a measure, once turned into a target, gets gamed directly, sometimes at the expense of the real goal it was meant to represent — exactly the deployment-frequency gaming example in the lesson.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a metric alone should not greenlight a roadmap item?
options: Because metrics should be combined with qualitative signals — interviews, support tickets, portal usage analytics — to confirm why something is happening before committing engineering time
Because metrics collected from CI runners and GitOps controllers are always inaccurate
Because DORA metrics are proprietary and cannot legally be used for internal prioritization
Because only the SPACE framework's Satisfaction dimension is trustworthy enough to act on alone
questions.explain: A metric tells you where to look, but triangulating it against qualitative signal — interviews, tickets, usage data — tells you why it's happening and whether the obvious fix is actually the right one.
